sections.body:
Sleep is not a switch that turns consciousness off. It is an active, organised state with its own architecture, and the body does specific jobs while you are in it.

The word covers two different things that alternate across the night. **Slow-wave sleep**, also called deep sleep, is the stage in which the body does its physical repair. Tissue is repaired, bone is rebuilt, and the immune system works through what the day has thrown at it. This is the stage that matters most if you are injured, ill, or training hard. **REM sleep**, where dreaming is most vivid, is when the brain processes the day: memory is consolidated, emotional reactions are dialled down, and the skill you practised in the afternoon is moved from temporary storage into something more permanent. Cutting either stage has consequences you can notice the next day.

The other work sleep does is regulation. While you sleep, your blood pressure falls, your heart rate slows, and your breathing settles. Your body temperature drops slightly and then climbs again before you wake. Blood sugar is held steadily. The brain clears out metabolic waste that accumulates during the day. Appetite hormones are reset, so the choices you make tomorrow morning are influenced by the night you had. Your stress hormones are brought back down.

Here is the part that surprises people: **poor sleep is a physical problem, not a discipline problem**. It is treated like a performance failure when it is closer to a supply problem. A person who cannot sleep because of a hot room, a noisy street, a new baby, a medication, pain, an overactive thyroid, or an anxiety disorder is not failing at something. They are dealing with a body that is being prevented from doing the one job it is trying to do.

And the effect runs both ways. Short sleep raises the risk of weight gain, high blood pressure, depression and reduced tolerance for alcohol. It worsens pain, which then worsens sleep. It makes you more likely to be irritable with your family, less accurate in your judgement, and slower to react while driving. None of this is a personality flaw. It is the predictable result of a system that has not had enough time to restore itself.

So the question is never whether you are tired. It is what your nights are actually doing for you, and whether the answer matches what your body needs.
examples: Sleep is when the body repairs itself and the brain files the day away.
I was not tired in the evening, I was tired in the morning, and that is a different problem.
sections.heading: What sleep actually is, and what it does for you

sections.body:
A normal night is not one long stretch of unconsciousness. It is four to six **cycles**, each lasting roughly ninety minutes, and each cycle passes through light sleep, deep sleep and REM sleep in a different order.

Deep sleep is front-loaded. In the first half of the night you spend more time in it, which is why a night of good sleep repairs more physical damage than the second half. REM sleep is back-loaded. The longest REM periods come in the last third of the night, which is why you dream vividly towards morning and why waking at six feels so much worse than waking at two.

The exact order of the stages is not fixed, and neither is the length of each cycle. The important thing is the shape of the night: **deep early, REM late, repeated four to six times**.

This is why waking in the middle of the night is normal rather than a sign of failure. In the lighter stages of sleep, the brain is briefly more responsive to sound and light, and it is quite possible to wake fully and not remember doing so. Most people wake once or twice a night and have no idea. **Waking and feeling unable to get back to sleep within twenty minutes** is a different situation, and one worth taking seriously if it happens most nights.

Two other facts about the architecture are useful. The body is very good at noticing a missed cycle, which is why you can sleep at the weekend and still feel groggy: you have shifted the clock, not repaid the debt. And the first ninety minutes after you fall asleep are the most valuable of the whole night, because that is where most of the deep sleep is. Going to bed two hours later does not move the deep sleep with you; it removes it.
examples: My sleep cycle is about ninety minutes, so I set my alarm for six hours rather than eight.
I wake at three most nights, but I fall back asleep within a few minutes.
Catching up at the weekend shifts my body clock, so Monday is hard.
sections.heading: The cycle, and why waking at three in the morning is normal

sections.body:
The widely used adult guidance is **seven to nine hours** of sleep in a 24-hour period, and most adults need somewhere in the middle of that range rather than at the top of it. Two points matter more than the number.

First, this is an average over a period, not a target for one night. One bad night costs you nothing much. A run of short nights costs a great deal, and the damage is cumulative.

Second, the number on the clock is not the same as the number of hours you were actually asleep. Time in bed is not sleep. If you lie awake for an hour getting up and going to the bathroom, that hour is not sleep, and it does not count towards your need. This is one reason that people who sleep nine hours in bed can still be sleep-deprived, and one reason that people with insomnia can be exhausted despite a long night.

You can check your own number without a gadget. The **sleep diary** is the standard clinical tool: for two weeks, you write down when you got into bed, when you estimated you fell asleep, when you woke, when you got up, whether you napped, and how you felt during the day. Two weeks is enough to see the pattern that one bad week hides. Sleep clinics use exactly this before they use anything else, and you can do it at home on a sheet of paper.

Other signs give you a rough estimate. If you need an alarm to wake up every morning, you are probably short. If you can sleep eight hours at the weekend without difficulty, your week is short. If you fall asleep within ten minutes of getting into bed and stay asleep, you are probably getting enough. If you are regularly sleepy in the afternoon, or you nod off while reading or driving, you are not.

Some people genuinely need less. A small number of people sleep five hours a night, fully awake, for years, with no impairment. It is rare, it usually runs in families, and it is worth checking with a doctor rather than assuming you are one of them, because the far more common explanation is that you have trained yourself to sleep less and have lost track of what you need.
examples: I was in bed for nine hours and asleep for seven, and the difference showed up in the morning.
I keep a two-week sleep diary, with the times written down each morning.
I need an alarm every morning, so my week is probably short.
sections.heading: How much sleep you actually need

sections.body:
The effects of short sleep are not just tiredness. They show up in judgement, mood, weight, blood pressure and safety, and they accumulate.

Judgement and reaction time. Sleep deprivation slows reaction time and reduces the accuracy of decisions that involve risk. The effect is largest in the tasks you are worst at, which is exactly the wrong direction. A tired driver does not notice that they are driving badly.

Mood. Sleep loss makes people more irritable, more anxious, and less able to read the emotion of others accurately. It also lowers the threshold for upset, so small problems feel larger. People who are sleep-deprived are more likely to describe an ambiguous situation as threatening. This is one of the more reliable findings in the field, and it explains why arguments at home so often happen after a bad night.

Weight and appetite. Short sleep raises the levels of hormones that drive hunger and lowers the hormone that signals fullness. People who are sleep-deprived also tend to prefer high-calorie, high-sugar food, and to eat later in the day. This is not a failure of willpower. It is hormone regulation working exactly as designed under a different condition.

Blood pressure and metabolism. Repeated short sleep is associated with higher blood pressure and with impaired glucose handling, which is why sleep is now routinely discussed alongside diet and exercise in any programme for metabolic health.

Pain. Sleep and pain amplify each other. Poor sleep lowers your pain threshold, and more pain disrupts sleep further. Anyone managing a chronic pain condition is usually told to treat sleep as part of the treatment rather than as a separate issue.

Immunity. A few nights of short sleep measurably reduces the body's ability to fight infection. People who are short of sleep catch the same cold more often, and take longer to shake it off.

The recovery is good news. A few nights of adequate sleep restores most of these measures reasonably quickly. The deficits that do not recover fully with a weekend lie elsewhere: they are the ones that come from months of short sleep rather than a bad Tuesday.
examples: After two short nights I was short-tempered with people I care about.
I was hungry all afternoon, and it turned out I had slept five hours.
My pain is worse on the nights I sleep badly, and the two feed each other.
sections.heading: What changes when sleep is too short

sections.body:
Most sleep problems are not mysterious. They are caused by a short list of habits, usually more than one, and they are fixable once you know which ones are working on you.

Caffeine is the biggest one, and it is the most misunderstood. Its half-life is about five to six hours, so a cup at 4 p.m. still leaves a meaningful dose in your system at 10 p.m. It does not only delay sleep onset; it reduces deep sleep even when you fall asleep quickly. Sources include tea, cola, energy drinks, chocolate and some painkillers. If you are sensitive, the effect can last eight hours or more.

Alcohol is the trap, because it helps you fall asleep. It sedates you quickly, so you feel the effect at once, but it suppresses REM sleep and fragments the second half of the night, which is when REM matters most. The result is a night that starts well and ends badly, with early waking and unrefreshing sleep. Alcohol also worsens snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea.

Light is powerful because it sets the clock. Bright light in the evening tells the body it is still daytime, and delays the release of melatonin, the hormone that signals the time to sleep. Screens are one source, but indoor lighting is another, and the morning matters just as much: strong light soon after waking helps set tonight's clock, while a dim morning and a bright evening pushes it the wrong way.

Screens also cost you in content. News, work messages and social feeds keep the mind alert, and the light is only part of the problem.

Timing is the quiet one. A body clock set by wake-up time, by light and by meals is remarkably regular, and it is disrupted by shift work, by late exercise, by late meals and by weekends that differ from weekdays by more than an hour.

The bedroom itself matters too: cool, dark and quiet, and used only for sleep and sex. If you work or watch television in bed, the bed stops being a signal for sleep.

Medical causes are worth ruling out if nothing else explains the problem: sleep apnoea, an overactive thyroid, pain, reflux, an enlarged prostate, restless legs, anaemia, depression and anxiety, and some medications including some decongestants, corticosteroids and certain antidepressants.
examples: I have moved my last coffee to noon, and the change took about a week.
I do not drink alcohol in the week now, and I sleep through the night again.
I put my phone in another room in the last hour before bed.
sections.heading: The saboteurs: caffeine, alcohol, light, screens and timing

sections.body:
Sleep has its own terms, and knowing them lets you describe the problem accurately to a doctor or to a pharmacist.

Circadian rhythm is the roughly 24-hour cycle that governs sleep, hormone release, body temperature and appetite. It is set mainly by light and is why your body wakes at a similar time on a free day.

Sleep onset latency is the time between getting into bed and falling asleep. Under about twenty minutes is normal. Over thirty minutes, most nights, is a common feature of insomnia.

Sleep efficiency is the proportion of time in bed that you were actually asleep. It is a useful number because a long night can still be a poor one. Above 85 % is generally good.

REM sleep is the dreaming stage, in which memory is consolidated and emotional reactions are regulated. **Sleep inertia** is the grogginess you feel in the first minutes after waking, which is worse when you wake from deep sleep, and which takes about fifteen minutes to clear.

Sleep debt is the accumulated shortfall against the amount you need. It can be partly repaid, but the recovery is slower than most people expect.

Insomnia is a difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early, that causes daytime impairment. The daytime impairment is part of the definition. Sleeping badly while feeling perfectly well is not insomnia.

Sleep apnoea is repeated pauses in breathing during sleep, usually with snoring and gasping. You usually cannot notice it yourself, which is why the person who sleeps next to you is often the one who notices.

Hypersomnia is sleeping much more than needed, and it is harder to recognise than short sleep because it is mistaken for laziness.
sections.heading: The vocabulary of sleep

terms.example: My circadian rhythm has shifted, because I have been going to bed at two every night.
terms.gloss: The roughly 24-hour cycle that sets your sleep, hormones, body temperature and appetite. Light is its strongest input.

terms.example: My sleep onset latency is about forty minutes, most nights.
terms.gloss: The time between getting into bed and falling asleep. Under about twenty minutes is normal.

terms.example: I was in bed for nine hours and my sleep efficiency was about seventy per cent.
terms.gloss: The share of your time in bed that you were actually asleep. A long night can still be an inefficient one.

terms.example: Alcohol takes away REM sleep, so I wake up tired even after a long night.
terms.gloss: The dreaming stage of sleep, when memory is consolidated and emotional reactions are regulated.

terms.example: I have been building up sleep debt for three weeks of early starts.
terms.gloss: The accumulated gap between the sleep you have had and the sleep you need. It can be partly repaid, but slowly.

terms.example: It is not just that I sleep badly; it is that I cannot work properly the next day. That makes it insomnia.
terms.gloss: Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early, together with daytime impairment. The daytime effect is part of the definition.

terms.example: My partner says I stop breathing in my sleep, so I will ask about sleep apnoea.
terms.gloss: Repeated pauses in breathing during sleep, usually with snoring and gasping. You usually cannot notice it yourself.

sections.body: A routine does not need to be elaborate. It needs to be repeatable on a Tuesday when you are tired, which is the only test that matters. Work backwards from the moment you want to be asleep, and choose a wake-up time first, because that is the anchor everything else hangs from.
examples: I keep my wake-up time to within thirty minutes, even after a late night.
If I am still awake after twenty minutes, I get up and read for a while.
I have moved my last coffee to eleven in the morning.
sections.heading: A wind-down routine you can keep on a working week
steps: Fix a wake-up time and keep it within the same hour every day, including at the weekend.
Get bright light within an hour of waking, and dim the lights in the last two hours before bed.
Move caffeine to before midday, and cut it entirely if you are sensitive.
Stop alcohol at least three hours before bed.
Finish exercise two to three hours before bed; a hard session right before does not help.
Put the phone in another room for the last hour, or at least out of reach of the pillow.
Keep the bedroom cool, dark and quiet, and use the bed only for sleep.
If you are awake and frustrated after about twenty minutes, get up, read something dull in low light, and return when sleepy.
Keep a two-week sleep diary and look at the pattern, not the bad nights.

sections.body:
I need eight hours exactly. The number that matters is your own, averaged over weeks, and it is a range rather than a rule. Chasing eight hours in bed when you need seven can create a problem where there was none.

If I am tired I will fall asleep straight away. Fatigue and sleepiness are not the same thing. Someone who is tired from a long day may lie awake for an hour because they are not sleepy enough to sleep, and the effort of trying makes it worse.

A nightcap helps me sleep. Alcohol shortens the time to fall asleep and damages the rest of the night, especially REM sleep. It also worsens snoring and sleep apnoea.

I can catch up at the weekend. You can partly recover, but a long lie-in shifts your body clock and the following week is harder, not easier. A consistent wake-up time is worth more than a long Saturday.

Snoring is harmless. Snoring can be a sign of repeated pauses in breathing, which raise blood pressure and leave you unrefreshed. If someone has noticed pauses or choking in your sleep, that is worth raising with a doctor.

Sleeping pills will fix it. Medicines for insomnia work for some people for a short period, and they are usually given alongside a routine, not instead of one. They are not a first answer, and some become hard to stop.
sections.heading: Sleep myths worth dropping

sections.body:
Most sleep problems improve with the routine changes above, given three to four weeks of genuine effort. Some do not, and the ones that do not need attention.

Go and see a doctor if you have been sleeping badly for **more than three months**, if it is affecting your work, your driving, or your mood, or if you have tried the routine changes and nothing has shifted. Also see a doctor rather than trying to fix it yourself if any of the following apply.

You **snore loudly and someone has noticed pauses in your breathing**, or you wake up gasping. This is the pattern of sleep apnoea, and it is common, treatable, and often missed because the person who has it is asleep while it happens.

You are **very sleepy during the day**, especially in situations that should keep you awake. If you fall asleep while driving, that is a safety issue and not something to wait on.

You **cannot sleep at all for several nights running**, or you sleep very little for no reason you can identify, with no tiredness during the day. That combination can point to a mood disorder or a medical cause.

You have **snapped out of sleep with a gasp or a pounding heart** several times a week. This can be sleep apnoea or another sleep-related breathing problem.

Your legs feel **restless or uncomfortable at night and you cannot settle them**, which points towards restless legs syndrome, which is treatable.

You have **lost your sense of smell or your sex drive**, or you feel unusually hot and cold in a pattern, or you have lost weight without trying. These can indicate thyroid problems or other medical causes of disrupted sleep.

Or your sleep has changed **after a new medicine**. Some medicines cause insomnia, some cause sleepiness, and a pharmacist can check the exact one you take in a few seconds.

When you go, bring your two-week sleep diary, and be ready to answer the same questions you prepared for a symptom history: when it started, what makes it worse, what you have tried, what medicines you take, and whether anyone else has noticed anything.
examples: My partner says I stop breathing in my sleep, and I snore loudly.
I have been sleeping badly for four months, and it is affecting my work.
I snap awake gasping a few times a week, and my heart is racing.
I have been keeping a sleep diary for two weeks, and I would like to go through it.
sections.heading: When poor sleep needs a doctor

item.summary: Sleep is not lost time. It is when your body repairs, consolidates memory and regulates mood. After reading this you can judge whether you are actually getting enough, understand what your sleep cycle does, remove the habits that quietly break your nights, build a wind-down routine that fits a real week, and know when poor sleep needs a doctor.
item.title: Why Sleep Matters More Than You Think
